newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia PM says Pol Pot used as bargaining chip.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia PM says Pol Pot used as bargaining chip.

text.p: Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh hinted on Friday that the Khmer Rouge guerrilla faction holding Pol Pot was using him as a bargaining chip in negotiations with the government.

He denied speculation in Phnom Penh that the negotiations with the splinter faction had stalled but said the leaders of the group were politically astute and the intense international attention on Pol Pot had strengthened their position.
"Politically, they are very mature, it is very serious," the prince told reporters.
"Now the world community is talking, talking without end about Pol Pot. Now Khieu Samphan, I feel, has clearly realised that he can get great advantage from Mr Pol Pot," the prince said.
Senior Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Samphan heads the rebel faction that broke with the notorious Pol Pot earlier this month and later detained him.

The Khmer Rouge were responsible for the 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror during which more than a million Cambodians died from execution, torture, disease or overwork in huge agricultural labour camps.

Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party has been negotiating with the breakaway rebel faction but the prince said on Friday there could be no agreement with the group until Khieu Samphan formally broke with Pol Pot and recognised the constitution of the country.

The prince said Khieu Samphan wanted to hold a news conference in Preah Vihear province in northern Cambodia on Saturday to formally announce the foundation of his Khmer Solidarity Party and make a declaration.
The prince said Khieu Samphan also wanted to tell the press that Pol Pot was "now completely finished".
But the prince said he would have nothing to do with any declaration Khieu Samphan might make, or meet him for talks, until Khieu Samphan cut himself from Pol Pot and recognised the constitution.
He said it was in Khieu Samphan's interests to hand Pol Pol over to the government as soon as possible.
"I hope that we will be able to take ...Pol Pot. I think so," the prince said.
The disintegrating Khmer Rouge guerrilla group has become a key factor in a long-running feud between Ranariddh and his uneasy coalition partner, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.
An alliance with the acceptable remnants of the guerrilla group could prove politically useful in the run-up to elections on May 23, political analysts said.
Hun Sen said on Friday he would welcome the Khmer Rouge remnants when they unconditionally dissolved their political and military organisations and handed Pol Pot to the government.

Ranariddh and Hun Sen share power in a coalition formed after 1993 elections supervised by the United Nations but relations between the two have been deteriorating since last year when Ranariddh demanded that he be given a greater share of power.
Political tension resulted last week in a battle on the streets of Phnom Penh between bodyguards loyal to the two prime ministers.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday cancelled a trip to Phnom Penh, citing security concerns.

Two envoys from the Group of Seven industrial countries had separate meetings with the two prime ministers on Thursday when they conveyed the group's concerns about Cambodia's political crisis, officials said.
Aides of both prime ministers said they both assured the envoys that they would work towards resolving their differences.
